title: Where you go
hook: Ruth to Naomi: where you go I will go

segments.voice: Yesterday, the command to love the stranger. Your line was you were strangers. Did a newcomer get a welcome from you? Today, a stranger who chose to stay. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

Three widows are standing on a road out of Moab. Naomi, the older one, has buried her husband and both her sons. Her two daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, have buried their husbands too. Naomi is heading home to Bethlehem, and she stops and tells the young women to turn around: "Go, return each to her mother's house." She has nothing left to give them. They cry. Orpah kisses her and goes. Ruth doesn't move. The King James puts it in a handful of words: "Ruth clave unto her." Today: what Ruth said next, and what it costs to stay.
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `ORPAH KISSES HER AND GOES.` → `RUTH DOESN'T MOVE.`

segments.voice: Start with the one who leaves, because the story is kind to her. Naomi asked both women to go, and she blessed them on the way: "the LORD deal kindly with you, as ye have dealt with the dead, and with me." Orpah does what she was asked. The text never scolds her. Going home was sensible, and it was allowed. That's what makes Ruth's choice stand out. She had an honorable way out, and she didn't take it. Look at the verb. "Ruth clave unto her." It's the same English verb the King James uses in Genesis for a man who will "cleave unto his wife." Clinging, holding on. Then she speaks. Earlier this year we heard her opening words, whither thou goest. Today, the line that follows them, which goes further: "Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried." Ruth isn't promising a trip. She's promising a whole life, and a grave, in a country where she will be the foreigner. Yesterday's stranger, seen from the other side. Notice what kind of promise it is. She doesn't talk about how she feels. She names a direction: where you go. And the story shows what that looks like on an ordinary day. In Bethlehem, Ruth goes out to glean, gathering leftover barley behind the reapers in someone else's field so the two of them can eat. Later the field's owner, Boaz, says something curious to her: "thou hast shewed more kindness in the latter end than at the beginning." The Hebrew word behind kindness there is chesed, the steady, loyal love we met at the start of this block. Some readers take that sentence as the book's quiet center: love that keeps going after the moment when leaving would have been fine.
screen: `ORPAH GOES, AND NO ONE BLAMES HER.` · `RUTH CLAVE UNTO HER.` · `WHERE THOU DIEST, WILL I DIE.` · `KINDNESS IN THE LATTER END.` · then, large: `WHERE YOU GO.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who is in a hard stretch right now, someone it would be easy, and even reasonable, to drift away from. Breathe, and let their face settle in front of you. Picture walking beside them for one more mile. You're not fixing anything. You're just staying. Then ask, quietly: what would staying look like this week? A call. A ride. An hour on their couch. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. Let the rest be quiet. The bell holds the time.
Where you go. Ruth's answer on the road: loyalty with a direction, staying when going home would have been allowed. Today's word.
Your line: where you go. Today, take one step toward the person you chose, a message or a visit, and stay a little longer than you planned. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Ruth's words to Naomi are read at some weddings and conversion ceremonies, and in Jewish communities the book of Ruth is read at the festival of Shavuot.

fork.setup: you're Naomi. two young widows are walking with you toward a country where you have nothing to give them. what do you do?
options: say nothing and let them come.
send them home, with a blessing.
make them promise never to leave.
fork.reveal: Naomi sends them back and blesses them: the LORD deal kindly with you. Orpah goes, and the text doesn't blame her. Ruth clings, and stays.

original.note: Hebrew: steady, loyal love; the word behind kindness when Boaz praises Ruth.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet line about going places together.
what it means: a widow choosing to stay with her mother-in-law, until death, in a land where she will be the foreigner.
what a scholar hears: chesed, the word Boaz uses for her kindness, loyalty that outlasts the moment when leaving was allowed.
